title: CBS Greenlights Drew Carey‑Hosted ‘Undercover Boss’ and Two Fresh Unscripted Series【Deadline】
body:
CBS has green‑lit three new unscripted series, marking the network’s most aggressive expansion of its reality‑programming slate in years. The centerpiece of the announcement is a refreshed version of the long‑running “Undercover Boss,” now fronted by comedian‑host Drew Carey, while the other two orders – “Stacks of Cash,” hosted by former “The Voice” judge Mike O’Malley, and “24 Hour Millionaire” – promise fresh twists on the high‑stakes, cash‑driven formats that have become staples of network television. The moves signal CBS’s intent to bolster its primetime schedule with cost‑effective, audience‑friendly fare as it competes with streaming services and a crowded broadcast landscape.

“Undercover Boss” first debuted on CBS in 2010 and quickly became a cultural touchstone, pairing executives who go incognito among their own employees with heartfelt moments of revelation and redemption. After a six‑year hiatus, the series will return with Carey, whose affable, every‑man persona is expected to inject a lighter, more comedic tone into the investigative premise. “Drew’s ability to connect with people on the shop floor and bring out genuine reactions is exactly what we need to revitalize the format,” a CBS executive said. The network hopes the new host will attract both nostalgic viewers and a younger demographic that appreciates Carey’s recent resurgence on talk‑show circuits and streaming platforms.

The second addition, “Stacks of Cash,” is positioned as a high‑energy competition where contestants battle through a series of increasingly difficult challenges to win stacks of money that are physically stacked on stage. Mike O’Malley, known for his sharp wit and experience as a talent coach, will guide participants and audience members through the gauntlet. Industry analysts note that the show’s premise taps into the current appetite for visually striking, fast‑paced game shows that can be easily packaged for digital clips and social‑media sharing. “The format is designed for binge‑watchability and viral moments,” said a television consultant familiar with the development. If successful, “Stacks of Cash” could become a staple for CBS’s Friday night lineup, a slot traditionally dominated by sitcoms and procedural dramas.

The third commission, “24 Hour Millionaire,” takes a different angle on the cash‑centric genre. Contestants are given a single day to turn a modest seed fund into a million dollars through a series of business‑related tasks, strategic investments, and entrepreneurial gambits. The format blends elements of reality competition with real‑world financial education, aiming to capture viewers who are fascinated by the hustle culture popularized by shows like “Shark Tank” and “The Profit.” The network plans to enlist a rotating panel of business experts to mentor participants, adding credibility and a learning component that could attract advertisers in the fintech and consumer‑finance sectors.

CBS’s decision to double down on unscripted content reflects broader industry trends. Production costs for reality formats are typically lower than scripted dramas, while the potential for high ratings and syndication revenue remains strong. Moreover, unscripted shows can be quickly adapted for streaming platforms, providing additional distribution avenues. The network’s recent ratings dip in scripted primetime slots has prompted executives to explore programming that can deliver reliable viewership with less financial risk. By pairing established names like Carey and O’Malley with innovative concepts, CBS hopes to rejuvenate its brand identity and reclaim a larger share of the advertising market.

Looking ahead, the success of these three series will likely influence CBS’s broader programming strategy. If the new “Undercover Boss” resonates with audiences, it could pave the way for further revivals of classic formats, while “Stacks of Cash” and “24 Hour Millionaire” may inspire spin‑offs or international adaptations. The network’s gamble on fresh unscripted content underscores a strategic pivot toward flexible, audience‑driven programming that can thrive across broadcast and digital ecosystems. As the fall schedule approaches, viewers and advertisers alike will be watching closely to see whether CBS’s renewed focus on reality television can deliver the ratings lift and cultural relevance the network seeks.
